Title: Will Big Tech’s troubles continue into 2023?
Text: [Yahoo Finance tech reporter Allie Garfinkle details the number of layoffs and hiring freezes that occurred at tech companies throughout 2022 and whether more should be expected in 2023.Video TranscriptSEANA SMITH: Big tech may be happy to see 2022 go, but after layoffs, regulatory scrutiny, and crashing stock prices, what lies ahead for the industry? Yahoo Finance's Allie Garfinkle joining us now with that look ahead. And Allie, I guess, what might 2023 look like?ALLIE GARFINKLE: You know, Seana, I think it's safe to say that a lot of what we've seen in 2022 is set to bleed into 2023. For instance, we're likely to see more layoffs, for example. And those hiring freezes that went into place a while ago at companies like, say, Google or Amazon, those will continue into next year.Companies are still contending with inflation, softening consumer demand, and frankly, a digital ad slowdown that has slammed even some of the biggest names in the business, like, for example, Meta, which laid off 10,000 employees-- I believe 13% of its corporate workforce just a couple of months ago. So there's that. I expect to see that continue.Another thing I actually also expect to see continuing is Washington. Washington stepped up its efforts to regulate big tech this year. And I don't think we're expecting to see that stop, right? For example, in the process right now, we have the FTC's attempts to block Microsoft's acquisition of Activision Blizzard, which is valued at $69 billion and Meta's acquisition of VR company Within. There's also-- now on top of all this, right, there's the ongoing battle over Section 230 and Google's fighting a lawsuit related to its search dominance. So there's a lot going on, on the Washington front. Expect to see things like layoffs and hiring freezes continue.But there is a kicker. And a lot of experts I talked to actually say that the second half of next year could bring better news for big tech. I'd love to use M&A as a case study. I used to be an M&A reporter, so it's my natural go-to. Look for a reset in tech M&A, for example, especially in Q3 and Q4.Private market deals are going to recover before the big public market deals, but we are going to see notable consolidation even from companies like Amazon or Microsoft as the year goes on in all likelihood. So I think the-- I think EY TMT leader Karl Chang summed it up best. He said he's going into this year looking at M&A and big tech overall, cautiously optimistic. And I would say that's the attitude we're bringing in right now.JARED BLIKRE: Allie, lots of people banking on that second half of 2023 turnaround. We'll have to see if it comes. Thank you for that report, Allie Garfinkle.]

Title: 2023 market recalibration process will ‘take a couple quarters to play out’: Strategist
Text: [BMO Wealth Management U.S. Chief Investment Strategist Yung-Yu Ma joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss the recent relief rally in markets, potential overhangs, Fed rate hikes in 2023, and the upcoming earnings season.Video TranscriptSEANA SMITH: It's great to see you again. So today's rally I guess a bit of good news here as we round out what has certainly been a very challenging year here for the markets. What does this signal to you in terms of what investors should expect as we look ahead to 2023?YUNG-YU MA: Hi, Seana. Thanks for having me again. It is nice to have a bit of a relief rally toward the end of the year. It's been a tough year, obviously. I wouldn't read too much into today's action. There is a lot of pessimism out there. So I think that does set up the market for sort of a snap-back rally at any given time.But we are in the heart of-- or approaching the heart of the time when we're going to get earnings warnings, and so that's going to cause an overhang in the markets until we get some more clarity and until the market can see some stabilization ahead.JARED BLIKRE: Let me ask you about that because you noted something-- I'm reading your notes right here-- something that's happened in the past two quarters that centers around earnings season. I'm always interested in seasonality plays here.YUNG-YU MA: Yeah, it's been interesting. Actually the past two quarters we've seen the market carve out a short-term bottom right about two weeks after the quarter end. So really right in the heart of those earnings warnings, the market had been declining and then stabilized as the market sort of sniffed out that the actual earnings might not be that bad.So we think there's a high chance that this quarter could be a repeat of that same scenario where we struggle for a few more weeks, but as we get closer and closer to the actual earnings reporting, things actually don't seem so bad. So that's something-- a pattern to look forward to that's played out the last couple of quarters.Story continuesSEANA SMITH: So Yung-Yu, do you, I guess, look at that type of bounce-- potential bounce in the markets as a buying opportunity here for investors?YUNG-YU MA: Well, we do think selloffs here are going to be buying opportunities, and that is based on our expectation of a soft landing in 2023. We do think the labor market will remain stable. We think that inflation is going to continue to come down. Consumers will see real wage gains, and corporations are not going to cut back all that much if spending is still pretty healthy in the economy.We just think that recalibration process is going to take a couple of quarters to play out. So we do think that to the extent that we see some downturns in the equity markets over the next few months that those are probably going to be buying opportunities.JARED BLIKRE: All right, you mentioned soft landing, so we've got to talk about the Fed. Big meeting end of January, early February, I believe. What are you expecting?YUNG-YU MA: Well, the Fed has definitely signaled a difficult path ahead. We actually think the Fed is overly hawkish and overly negative in some of its projections in terms of higher inflation, slower growth, higher unemployment. We don't think that's actually going to come to pass in terms of unemployment shooting up as much as the Fed is expecting.So in the coming meeting, we think the Fed will probably soften its tone a little bit if inflation continues to come down, as it has been-- the data has actually been reasonably good for inflation-- and if we see that the labor market, at least at the edges, is softening a bit, which we are seeing, a still healthy labor market but that's softening around the edges.SEANA SMITH: So Yung-Yu, then how many more hikes do you think are likely on the table then before the Fed maybe pauses?YUNG-YU MA: Maybe another 1/2%. We think that's probably par for the course. Perhaps 1/4% the next meeting, maybe 1/2%. But overall, we think the Fed is going to pause right around 5% in terms of the fed funds rate and hold it there for quite some time.Could it be another 1/2%? Could it be another 3/4% on the upside if we get some negative inflation data? Both of those are possible, but right around 5% is where we see somewhat of a steady state for 2023.JARED BLIKRE: And when we look inside the market, what are you looking at specifically in terms of sectors, styles? Any positions that you're interested or areas of the market you're interested in the new year?YUNG-YU MA: Yeah, Jared, there definitely are. We actually think much of the plays that revolve around infrastructure have a lot of runway to them and a lot of legs. And that, of course, spans a few different sectors-- some areas of industrials, some areas of materials. But we have a lot of money that's going to flow into the economy from the Infrastructure Act, from the CHIPS Act, from the Inflation Reduction Act, and that's going to create-- you know, there are hundreds of billions of dollars of spending that are going to flow through the economy over the next few years, and we think that provides a nice runway for infrastructure.We also think biotech is probably likely to have a good year. There have been a lot of major platform developments we think are going to continue to play out in the biotech sector. So we think that's actually an area of outperformance for 2023.And I'd say a third area to pay attention to overall is just value. We think that value over growth has a long runway to it as well. So low P/E multiples, stable businesses returning cash flow or buying back shares, increasing their dividends, those areas of value that really look more stable we think have a nice trajectory to them as well.SEANA SMITH: Yung-Yu, you mentioned earnings warnings. We certainly have seen the estimates lowered for 2023. When do you expect earnings to then stabilize potentially?YUNG-YU MA: We do expect them to stabilize, and that's part of our soft-landing thesis. We think this recalibration probably has another quarter or two to go in terms of seeing pretty meaningful earnings cuts over this coming quarter and also the second quarter. But into the back half of the year, we think those earnings will stabilize, and we think the market will probably catch wind of that early in 2023. So we're expecting choppiness in the near term, but we expect-- our expectation of those stable earnings should filter through into a stable market in the coming months.]

Title: Best Performing ETFs of 2022
Text: [If you guessed at the start of the year—before war, inflation and rate hikes—which funds would turn in the best annual performance, maybe you would have said broad stock indexes, real estate or bonds.You would have been wrong.The top-performing ETF of 2022, once you filter out leveraged and inverse products, was the $424.2 million iShares MSCI Turkey ETF (TUR) with a monster return of 104% through Dec. 27.Turkey’s lira plummeted during the year while inflation soared as high as 80%. However, that was what drove the stock market’s outstanding performance, as domestic investors plowed in assets to hedge against skyrocketing prices.Despite its outsized returns, U.S. investors aren’t taking the bait, and the fund has seen $82.8 million in outflows year-to-date. Indeed, a recent Bloomberg article notes that foreign ownership of Turkish stocks hit record lows.The runner up to TUR is the $375.9 million Simplify Interest Rate Hedge ETF (PFIX), which rolled out in May 2021. The fund is designed to provide a hedge against sharp increases in interest rates, which it does by holding U.S. Treasury securities and U.S. Treasury Inflation Protected Securities in conjunction with interest rate options. Title: 2023 market recalibration process will ‘take a couple quarters to play out’: Strategist
Text: [BMO Wealth Management U.S. Chief Investment Strategist Yung-Yu Ma joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss the recent relief rally in markets, potential overhangs, Fed rate hikes in 2023, and the upcoming earnings season.Video TranscriptSEANA SMITH: It's great to see you again. So today's rally I guess a bit of good news here as we round out what has certainly been a very challenging year here for the markets. What does this signal to you in terms of what investors should expect as we look ahead to 2023?YUNG-YU MA: Hi, Seana. Thanks for having me again. It is nice to have a bit of a relief rally toward the end of the year. It's been a tough year, obviously. I wouldn't read too much into today's action. There is a lot of pessimism out there. So I think that does set up the market for sort of a snap-back rally at any given time.But we are in the heart of-- or approaching the heart of the time when we're going to get earnings warnings, and so that's going to cause an overhang in the markets until we get some more clarity and until the market can see some stabilization ahead.JARED BLIKRE: Let me ask you about that because you noted something-- I'm reading your notes right here-- something that's happened in the past two quarters that centers around earnings season. I'm always interested in seasonality plays here.YUNG-YU MA: Yeah, it's been interesting. Actually the past two quarters we've seen the market carve out a short-term bottom right about two weeks after the quarter end. So really right in the heart of those earnings warnings, the market had been declining and then stabilized as the market sort of sniffed out that the actual earnings might not be that bad.So we think there's a high chance that this quarter could be a repeat of that same scenario where we struggle for a few more weeks, but as we get closer and closer to the actual earnings reporting, things actually don't seem so bad. So that's something-- a pattern to look forward to that's played out the last couple of quarters.Story continuesSEANA SMITH: So Yung-Yu, do you, I guess, look at that type of bounce-- potential bounce in the markets as a buying opportunity here for investors?YUNG-YU MA: Well, we do think selloffs here are going to be buying opportunities, and that is based on our expectation of a soft landing in 2023. We do think the labor market will remain stable. We think that inflation is going to continue to come down. Consumers will see real wage gains, and corporations are not going to cut back all that much if spending is still pretty healthy in the economy.We just think that recalibration process is going to take a couple of quarters to play out. So we do think that to the extent that we see some downturns in the equity markets over the next few months that those are probably going to be buying opportunities.JARED BLIKRE: All right, you mentioned soft landing, so we've got to talk about the Fed. Big meeting end of January, early February, I believe. What are you expecting?YUNG-YU MA: Well, the Fed has definitely signaled a difficult path ahead. We actually think the Fed is overly hawkish and overly negative in some of its projections in terms of higher inflation, slower growth, higher unemployment. We don't think that's actually going to come to pass in terms of unemployment shooting up as much as the Fed is expecting.So in the coming meeting, we think the Fed will probably soften its tone a little bit if inflation continues to come down, as it has been-- the data has actually been reasonably good for inflation-- and if we see that the labor market, at least at the edges, is softening a bit, which we are seeing, a still healthy labor market but that's softening around the edges.SEANA SMITH: So Yung-Yu, then how many more hikes do you think are likely on the table then before the Fed maybe pauses?YUNG-YU MA: Maybe another 1/2%. We think that's probably par for the course. Perhaps 1/4% the next meeting, maybe 1/2%. But overall, we think the Fed is going to pause right around 5% in terms of the fed funds rate and hold it there for quite some time.Could it be another 1/2%? Could it be another 3/4% on the upside if we get some negative inflation data? Both of those are possible, but right around 5% is where we see somewhat of a steady state for 2023.JARED BLIKRE: And when we look inside the market, what are you looking at specifically in terms of sectors, styles? Any positions that you're interested or areas of the market you're interested in the new year?YUNG-YU MA: Yeah, Jared, there definitely are. We actually think much of the plays that revolve around infrastructure have a lot of runway to them and a lot of legs. And that, of course, spans a few different sectors-- some areas of industrials, some areas of materials. But we have a lot of money that's going to flow into the economy from the Infrastructure Act, from the CHIPS Act, from the Inflation Reduction Act, and that's going to create-- you know, there are hundreds of billions of dollars of spending that are going to flow through the economy over the next few years, and we think that provides a nice runway for infrastructure.We also think biotech is probably likely to have a good year. There have been a lot of major platform developments we think are going to continue to play out in the biotech sector. So we think that's actually an area of outperformance for 2023.And I'd say a third area to pay attention to overall is just value. We think that value over growth has a long runway to it as well. So low P/E multiples, stable businesses returning cash flow or buying back shares, increasing their dividends, those areas of value that really look more stable we think have a nice trajectory to them as well.SEANA SMITH: Yung-Yu, you mentioned earnings warnings. We certainly have seen the estimates lowered for 2023. When do you expect earnings to then stabilize potentially?YUNG-YU MA: We do expect them to stabilize, and that's part of our soft-landing thesis. We think this recalibration probably has another quarter or two to go in terms of seeing pretty meaningful earnings cuts over this coming quarter and also the second quarter. But into the back half of the year, we think those earnings will stabilize, and we think the market will probably catch wind of that early in 2023. So we're expecting choppiness in the near term, but we expect-- our expectation of those stable earnings should filter through into a stable market in the coming months.]

Title: 2023 market recalibration process will ‘take a couple quarters to play out’: Strategist
Text: [BMO Wealth Management U.S. Chief Investment Strategist Yung-Yu Ma joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss the recent relief rally in markets, potential overhangs, Fed rate hikes in 2023, and the upcoming earnings season.Video TranscriptSEANA SMITH: It's great to see you again. So today's rally I guess a bit of good news here as we round out what has certainly been a very challenging year here for the markets. What does this signal to you in terms of what investors should expect as we look ahead to 2023?YUNG-YU MA: Hi, Seana. Thanks for having me again. It is nice to have a bit of a relief rally toward the end of the year. It's been a tough year, obviously. I wouldn't read too much into today's action. There is a lot of pessimism out there. So I think that does set up the market for sort of a snap-back rally at any given time.But we are in the heart of-- or approaching the heart of the time when we're going to get earnings warnings, and so that's going to cause an overhang in the markets until we get some more clarity and until the market can see some stabilization ahead.JARED BLIKRE: Let me ask you about that because you noted something-- I'm reading your notes right here-- something that's happened in the past two quarters that centers around earnings season. I'm always interested in seasonality plays here.YUNG-YU MA: Yeah, it's been interesting. Actually the past two quarters we've seen the market carve out a short-term bottom right about two weeks after the quarter end. So really right in the heart of those earnings warnings, the market had been declining and then stabilized as the market sort of sniffed out that the actual earnings might not be that bad.So we think there's a high chance that this quarter could be a repeat of that same scenario where we struggle for a few more weeks, but as we get closer and closer to the actual earnings reporting, things actually don't seem so bad. So that's something-- a pattern to look forward to that's played out the last couple of quarters.Story continuesSEANA SMITH: So Yung-Yu, do you, I guess, look at that type of bounce-- potential bounce in the markets as a buying opportunity here for investors?YUNG-YU MA: Well, we do think selloffs here are going to be buying opportunities, and that is based on our expectation of a soft landing in 2023. We do think the labor market will remain stable. We think that inflation is going to continue to come down. Consumers will see real wage gains, and corporations are not going to cut back all that much if spending is still pretty healthy in the economy.We just think that recalibration process is going to take a couple of quarters to play out. So we do think that to the extent that we see some downturns in the equity markets over the next few months that those are probably going to be buying opportunities.JARED BLIKRE: All right, you mentioned soft landing, so we've got to talk about the Fed. Big meeting end of January, early February, I believe. What are you expecting?YUNG-YU MA: Well, the Fed has definitely signaled a difficult path ahead. We actually think the Fed is overly hawkish and overly negative in some of its projections in terms of higher inflation, slower growth, higher unemployment. We don't think that's actually going to come to pass in terms of unemployment shooting up as much as the Fed is expecting.So in the coming meeting, we think the Fed will probably soften its tone a little bit if inflation continues to come down, as it has been-- the data has actually been reasonably good for inflation-- and if we see that the labor market, at least at the edges, is softening a bit, which we are seeing, a still healthy labor market but that's softening around the edges.SEANA SMITH: So Yung-Yu, then how many more hikes do you think are likely on the table then before the Fed maybe pauses?YUNG-YU MA: Maybe another 1/2%. We think that's probably par for the course. Perhaps 1/4% the next meeting, maybe 1/2%. But overall, we think the Fed is going to pause right around 5% in terms of the fed funds rate and hold it there for quite some time.Could it be another 1/2%? Could it be another 3/4% on the upside if we get some negative inflation data? Both of those are possible, but right around 5% is where we see somewhat of a steady state for 2023.JARED BLIKRE: And when we look inside the market, what are you looking at specifically in terms of sectors, styles? Any positions that you're interested or areas of the market you're interested in the new year?YUNG-YU MA: Yeah, Jared, there definitely are. We actually think much of the plays that revolve around infrastructure have a lot of runway to them and a lot of legs. And that, of course, spans a few different sectors-- some areas of industrials, some areas of materials. But we have a lot of money that's going to flow into the economy from the Infrastructure Act, from the CHIPS Act, from the Inflation Reduction Act, and that's going to create-- you know, there are hundreds of billions of dollars of spending that are going to flow through the economy over the next few years, and we think that provides a nice runway for infrastructure.We also think biotech is probably likely to have a good year. There have been a lot of major platform developments we think are going to continue to play out in the biotech sector. So we think that's actually an area of outperformance for 2023.And I'd say a third area to pay attention to overall is just value. We think that value over growth has a long runway to it as well. So low P/E multiples, stable businesses returning cash flow or buying back shares, increasing their dividends, those areas of value that really look more stable we think have a nice trajectory to them as well.SEANA SMITH: Yung-Yu, you mentioned earnings warnings. We certainly have seen the estimates lowered for 2023. When do you expect earnings to then stabilize potentially?YUNG-YU MA: We do expect them to stabilize, and that's part of our soft-landing thesis. We think this recalibration probably has another quarter or two to go in terms of seeing pretty meaningful earnings cuts over this coming quarter and also the second quarter. But into the back half of the year, we think those earnings will stabilize, and we think the market will probably catch wind of that early in 2023. So we're expecting choppiness in the near term, but we expect-- our expectation of those stable earnings should filter through into a stable market in the coming months.]

Title: Best Performing ETFs of 2022
Text: [If you guessed at the start of the year—before war, inflation and rate hikes—which funds would turn in the best annual performance, maybe you would have said broad stock indexes, real estate or bonds.You would have been wrong.The top-performing ETF of 2022, once you filter out leveraged and inverse products, was the $424.2 million iShares MSCI Turkey ETF (TUR) with a monster return of 104% through Dec. 27.Turkey’s lira plummeted during the year while inflation soared as high as 80%. However, that was what drove the stock market’s outstanding performance, as domestic investors plowed in assets to hedge against skyrocketing prices.Despite its outsized returns, U.S. investors aren’t taking the bait, and the fund has seen $82.8 million in outflows year-to-date. Indeed, a recent Bloomberg article notes that foreign ownership of Turkish stocks hit record lows.The runner up to TUR is the $375.9 million Simplify Interest Rate Hedge ETF (PFIX), which rolled out in May 2021. The fund is designed to provide a hedge against sharp increases in interest rates, which it does by holding U.S. Treasury securities and U.S. Treasury Inflation Protected Securities in conjunction with interest rate options. PFIX is up 93% this year, and unlike TUR, it has seen inflows to the tune of $123.3 million.Energy All the Way Down From PFIX on down, the top performers are energy related with one exception. The $2.6 billion VanEck Oil Services ETF (OIH) was in the No. 3 spot with a gain of 66%, followed by the $40.7 billion Energy Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLE) with a return of 65%.Ultimately the remaining energy funds in the top 20 ETFs in terms of returns were up anywhere from 49% (the Invesco DWA Energy Momentum ETF (PXI)) to 65% (the iShares U.S. Oil Equipment & Services ETF (IEZ)). Almost all of those were equity funds; however, the United States 12-Month Natural Gas Fund LP (UNL) was in the mix with a return of 57%. The fund invests in natural gas futures via a laddered strategy that maintains equal-weight exposure to the 12 nearest-month NYMEX natural gas futures.Story continuesAccording to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, energy costs for Americans saw an average increase of 13% year-over-year as of November.Nickel Another Outlier Nestled in the No. 19 spot for returns is the $43.7 million iPath Series B Bloomberg Nickel Subindex Total Return ETN (JJN) with a return of 50%. The ETN, which tracks the price of nickel futures, saw a sharp spike back in early March before falling almost as dramatically, but it climbed fairly steadily during the final quarter. Demand for nickel has seen an increase largely due to its use in batteries for electric vehicles, and that demand is expected to continue to grow over the next few years. FundTickerYTD ReturniShares MSCI Turkey ETFTUR104.0%Simplify Interest Rate Hedge ETFPFIX93.0%VanEck Oil Services ETFOIH66.0%Energy Select Sector SPDR FundXLE65.2%iShares U.S. Oil Equipment & Services ETFIEZ64.9%Fidelity MSCI Energy Index ETFFENY64.4%Vanguard Energy ETFVDE64.2%Invesco Dynamic Energy Exploration & Production ETFPXE61.5%Invesco Dynamic Oil & Gas Services ETFPXJ60.9%Credit Suisse S&P MLP Index ETNMLPO60.6%SPDR S&P Oil & Gas Equipment & Services ETFXES60.6%iShares U.S. Energy ETFIYE60.2%Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight Energy ETFRYE59.7%iShares U.S. Oil & Gas Exploration & Production ETFIEO58.8%United States 12 Month Natural Gas Fund LPUNL57.1%First Trust Natural Gas ETFFCG50.3%First Trust Energy AlphaDEX FundFXN50.0%iShares Global Energy ETFIXC49.6%iPath Series B Bloomberg Nickel Subindex Total Return ETNJJN49.5%Invesco DWA Energy Momentum ETFPXI49.5%Source: FactSet, data as of Dec. 27, 2022 Contact Heather Bell at heather.bell@etf.com Recommended StoriesETF Industry’s $1T Mutual Fund Grab: Part 1 Buffered ETFs’ $10 Billion YearHot Reads: The Trouble With TechHot Reads: The Crypto Contagion ContinuesPermalink | © Copyright 2022 ETF.com. Title: 2023 market recalibration process will ‘take a couple quarters to play out’: Strategist
Text: [BMO Wealth Management U.S. Chief Investment Strategist Yung-Yu Ma joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss the recent relief rally in markets, potential overhangs, Fed rate hikes in 2023, and the upcoming earnings season.Video TranscriptSEANA SMITH: It's great to see you again. So today's rally I guess a bit of good news here as we round out what has certainly been a very challenging year here for the markets. What does this signal to you in terms of what investors should expect as we look ahead to 2023?YUNG-YU MA: Hi, Seana. Thanks for having me again. It is nice to have a bit of a relief rally toward the end of the year. It's been a tough year, obviously. I wouldn't read too much into today's action. There is a lot of pessimism out there. So I think that does set up the market for sort of a snap-back rally at any given time.But we are in the heart of-- or approaching the heart of the time when we're going to get earnings warnings, and so that's going to cause an overhang in the markets until we get some more clarity and until the market can see some stabilization ahead.JARED BLIKRE: Let me ask you about that because you noted something-- I'm reading your notes right here-- something that's happened in the past two quarters that centers around earnings season. I'm always interested in seasonality plays here.YUNG-YU MA: Yeah, it's been interesting. Actually the past two quarters we've seen the market carve out a short-term bottom right about two weeks after the quarter end. So really right in the heart of those earnings warnings, the market had been declining and then stabilized as the market sort of sniffed out that the actual earnings might not be that bad.So we think there's a high chance that this quarter could be a repeat of that same scenario where we struggle for a few more weeks, but as we get closer and closer to the actual earnings reporting, things actually don't seem so bad. So that's something-- a pattern to look forward to that's played out the last couple of quarters.Story continuesSEANA SMITH: So Yung-Yu, do you, I guess, look at that type of bounce-- potential bounce in the markets as a buying opportunity here for investors?YUNG-YU MA: Well, we do think selloffs here are going to be buying opportunities, and that is based on our expectation of a soft landing in 2023. We do think the labor market will remain stable. We think that inflation is going to continue to come down. Consumers will see real wage gains, and corporations are not going to cut back all that much if spending is still pretty healthy in the economy.We just think that recalibration process is going to take a couple of quarters to play out. So we do think that to the extent that we see some downturns in the equity markets over the next few months that those are probably going to be buying opportunities.JARED BLIKRE: All right, you mentioned soft landing, so we've got to talk about the Fed. Big meeting end of January, early February, I believe. What are you expecting?YUNG-YU MA: Well, the Fed has definitely signaled a difficult path ahead. We actually think the Fed is overly hawkish and overly negative in some of its projections in terms of higher inflation, slower growth, higher unemployment. We don't think that's actually going to come to pass in terms of unemployment shooting up as much as the Fed is expecting.So in the coming meeting, we think the Fed will probably soften its tone a little bit if inflation continues to come down, as it has been-- the data has actually been reasonably good for inflation-- and if we see that the labor market, at least at the edges, is softening a bit, which we are seeing, a still healthy labor market but that's softening around the edges.SEANA SMITH: So Yung-Yu, then how many more hikes do you think are likely on the table then before the Fed maybe pauses?YUNG-YU MA: Maybe another 1/2%. We think that's probably par for the course. Perhaps 1/4% the next meeting, maybe 1/2%. But overall, we think the Fed is going to pause right around 5% in terms of the fed funds rate and hold it there for quite some time.Could it be another 1/2%? Could it be another 3/4% on the upside if we get some negative inflation data? Both of those are possible, but right around 5% is where we see somewhat of a steady state for 2023.JARED BLIKRE: And when we look inside the market, what are you looking at specifically in terms of sectors, styles? Any positions that you're interested or areas of the market you're interested in the new year?YUNG-YU MA: Yeah, Jared, there definitely are. We actually think much of the plays that revolve around infrastructure have a lot of runway to them and a lot of legs. And that, of course, spans a few different sectors-- some areas of industrials, some areas of materials. But we have a lot of money that's going to flow into the economy from the Infrastructure Act, from the CHIPS Act, from the Inflation Reduction Act, and that's going to create-- you know, there are hundreds of billions of dollars of spending that are going to flow through the economy over the next few years, and we think that provides a nice runway for infrastructure.We also think biotech is probably likely to have a good year. There have been a lot of major platform developments we think are going to continue to play out in the biotech sector. So we think that's actually an area of outperformance for 2023.And I'd say a third area to pay attention to overall is just value. We think that value over growth has a long runway to it as well. So low P/E multiples, stable businesses returning cash flow or buying back shares, increasing their dividends, those areas of value that really look more stable we think have a nice trajectory to them as well.SEANA SMITH: Yung-Yu, you mentioned earnings warnings. We certainly have seen the estimates lowered for 2023. When do you expect earnings to then stabilize potentially?YUNG-YU MA: We do expect them to stabilize, and that's part of our soft-landing thesis. We think this recalibration probably has another quarter or two to go in terms of seeing pretty meaningful earnings cuts over this coming quarter and also the second quarter. But into the back half of the year, we think those earnings will stabilize, and we think the market will probably catch wind of that early in 2023. So we're expecting choppiness in the near term, but we expect-- our expectation of those stable earnings should filter through into a stable market in the coming months.]

Title: Best Performing ETFs of 2022
Text: [If you guessed at the start of the year—before war, inflation and rate hikes—which funds would turn in the best annual performance, maybe you would have said broad stock indexes, real estate or bonds.You would have been wrong.The top-performing ETF of 2022, once you filter out leveraged and inverse products, was the $424.2 million iShares MSCI Turkey ETF (TUR) with a monster return of 104% through Dec. 27.Turkey’s lira plummeted during the year while inflation soared as high as 80%. However, that was what drove the stock market’s outstanding performance, as domestic investors plowed in assets to hedge against skyrocketing prices.Despite its outsized returns, U.S. investors aren’t taking the bait, and the fund has seen $82.8 million in outflows year-to-date. Indeed, a recent Bloomberg article notes that foreign ownership of Turkish stocks hit record lows.The runner up to TUR is the $375.9 million Simplify Interest Rate Hedge ETF (PFIX), which rolled out in May 2021. The fund is designed to provide a hedge against sharp increases in interest rates, which it does by holding U.S. Treasury securities and U.S. Treasury Inflation Protected Securities in conjunction with interest rate options. PFIX is up 93% this year, and unlike TUR, it has seen inflows to the tune of $123.3 million.Energy All the Way Down From PFIX on down, the top performers are energy related with one exception. The $2.6 billion VanEck Oil Services ETF (OIH) was in the No. 3 spot with a gain of 66%, followed by the $40.7 billion Energy Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLE) with a return of 65%.Ultimately the remaining energy funds in the top 20 ETFs in terms of returns were up anywhere from 49% (the Invesco DWA Energy Momentum ETF (PXI)) to 65% (the iShares U.S. Oil Equipment & Services ETF (IEZ)). Almost all of those were equity funds; however, the United States 12-Month Natural Gas Fund LP (UNL) was in the mix with a return of 57%. The fund invests in natural gas futures via a laddered strategy that maintains equal-weight exposure to the 12 nearest-month NYMEX natural gas futures.Story continuesAccording to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, energy costs for Americans saw an average increase of 13% year-over-year as of November.Nickel Another Outlier Nestled in the No. 19 spot for returns is the $43.7 million iPath Series B Bloomberg Nickel Subindex Total Return ETN (JJN) with a return of 50%. The ETN, which tracks the price of nickel futures, saw a sharp spike back in early March before falling almost as dramatically, but it climbed fairly steadily during the final quarter. Demand for nickel has seen an increase largely due to its use in batteries for electric vehicles, and that demand is expected to continue to grow over the next few years. FundTickerYTD ReturniShares MSCI Turkey ETFTUR104.0%Simplify Interest Rate Hedge ETFPFIX93.0%VanEck Oil Services ETFOIH66.0%Energy Select Sector SPDR FundXLE65.2%iShares U.S. Oil Equipment & Services ETFIEZ64.9%Fidelity MSCI Energy Index ETFFENY64.4%Vanguard Energy ETFVDE64.2%Invesco Dynamic Energy Exploration & Production ETFPXE61.5%Invesco Dynamic Oil & Gas Services ETFPXJ60.9%Credit Suisse S&P MLP Index ETNMLPO60.6%SPDR S&P Oil & Gas Equipment & Services ETFXES60.6%iShares U.S. Energy ETFIYE60.2%Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight Energy ETFRYE59.7%iShares U.S. Oil & Gas Exploration & Production ETFIEO58.8%United States 12 Month Natural Gas Fund LPUNL57.1%First Trust Natural Gas ETFFCG50.3%First Trust Energy AlphaDEX FundFXN50.0%iShares Global Energy ETFIXC49.6%iPath Series B Bloomberg Nickel Subindex Total Return ETNJJN49.5%Invesco DWA Energy Momentum ETFPXI49.5%Source: FactSet, data as of Dec. 27, 2022 Contact Heather Bell at heather.bell@etf.com Recommended StoriesETF Industry’s $1T Mutual Fund Grab: Part 1 Buffered ETFs’ $10 Billion YearHot Reads: The Trouble With TechHot Reads: The Crypto Contagion ContinuesPermalink | © Copyright 2022 ETF.com. Title: 2023 market recalibration process will ‘take a couple quarters to play out’: Strategist
Text: [BMO Wealth Management U.S. Chief Investment Strategist Yung-Yu Ma joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss the recent relief rally in markets, potential overhangs, Fed rate hikes in 2023, and the upcoming earnings season.Video TranscriptSEANA SMITH: It's great to see you again. So today's rally I guess a bit of good news here as we round out what has certainly been a very challenging year here for the markets. What does this signal to you in terms of what investors should expect as we look ahead to 2023?YUNG-YU MA: Hi, Seana. Thanks for having me again. It is nice to have a bit of a relief rally toward the end of the year. It's been a tough year, obviously. I wouldn't read too much into today's action. There is a lot of pessimism out there. So I think that does set up the market for sort of a snap-back rally at any given time.But we are in the heart of-- or approaching the heart of the time when we're going to get earnings warnings, and so that's going to cause an overhang in the markets until we get some more clarity and until the market can see some stabilization ahead.JARED BLIKRE: Let me ask you about that because you noted something-- I'm reading your notes right here-- something that's happened in the past two quarters that centers around earnings season. I'm always interested in seasonality plays here.YUNG-YU MA: Yeah, it's been interesting. Actually the past two quarters we've seen the market carve out a short-term bottom right about two weeks after the quarter end. So really right in the heart of those earnings warnings, the market had been declining and then stabilized as the market sort of sniffed out that the actual earnings might not be that bad.So we think there's a high chance that this quarter could be a repeat of that same scenario where we struggle for a few more weeks, but as we get closer and closer to the actual earnings reporting, things actually don't seem so bad. So that's something-- a pattern to look forward to that's played out the last couple of quarters.Story continuesSEANA SMITH: So Yung-Yu, do you, I guess, look at that type of bounce-- potential bounce in the markets as a buying opportunity here for investors?YUNG-YU MA: Well, we do think selloffs here are going to be buying opportunities, and that is based on our expectation of a soft landing in 2023. We do think the labor market will remain stable. We think that inflation is going to continue to come down. Consumers will see real wage gains, and corporations are not going to cut back all that much if spending is still pretty healthy in the economy.We just think that recalibration process is going to take a couple of quarters to play out. So we do think that to the extent that we see some downturns in the equity markets over the next few months that those are probably going to be buying opportunities.JARED BLIKRE: All right, you mentioned soft landing, so we've got to talk about the Fed. Big meeting end of January, early February, I believe. What are you expecting?YUNG-YU MA: Well, the Fed has definitely signaled a difficult path ahead. We actually think the Fed is overly hawkish and overly negative in some of its projections in terms of higher inflation, slower growth, higher unemployment. We don't think that's actually going to come to pass in terms of unemployment shooting up as much as the Fed is expecting.So in the coming meeting, we think the Fed will probably soften its tone a little bit if inflation continues to come down, as it has been-- the data has actually been reasonably good for inflation-- and if we see that the labor market, at least at the edges, is softening a bit, which we are seeing, a still healthy labor market but that's softening around the edges.SEANA SMITH: So Yung-Yu, then how many more hikes do you think are likely on the table then before the Fed maybe pauses?YUNG-YU MA: Maybe another 1/2%. We think that's probably par for the course. Perhaps 1/4% the next meeting, maybe 1/2%. But overall, we think the Fed is going to pause right around 5% in terms of the fed funds rate and hold it there for quite some time.Could it be another 1/2%? Could it be another 3/4% on the upside if we get some negative inflation data? Both of those are possible, but right around 5% is where we see somewhat of a steady state for 2023.JARED BLIKRE: And when we look inside the market, what are you looking at specifically in terms of sectors, styles? Any positions that you're interested or areas of the market you're interested in the new year?YUNG-YU MA: Yeah, Jared, there definitely are. We actually think much of the plays that revolve around infrastructure have a lot of runway to them and a lot of legs. And that, of course, spans a few different sectors-- some areas of industrials, some areas of materials. But we have a lot of money that's going to flow into the economy from the Infrastructure Act, from the CHIPS Act, from the Inflation Reduction Act, and that's going to create-- you know, there are hundreds of billions of dollars of spending that are going to flow through the economy over the next few years, and we think that provides a nice runway for infrastructure.We also think biotech is probably likely to have a good year. There have been a lot of major platform developments we think are going to continue to play out in the biotech sector. So we think that's actually an area of outperformance for 2023.And I'd say a third area to pay attention to overall is just value. We think that value over growth has a long runway to it as well. So low P/E multiples, stable businesses returning cash flow or buying back shares, increasing their dividends, those areas of value that really look more stable we think have a nice trajectory to them as well.SEANA SMITH: Yung-Yu, you mentioned earnings warnings. We certainly have seen the estimates lowered for 2023. When do you expect earnings to then stabilize potentially?YUNG-YU MA: We do expect them to stabilize, and that's part of our soft-landing thesis. We think this recalibration probably has another quarter or two to go in terms of seeing pretty meaningful earnings cuts over this coming quarter and also the second quarter. But into the back half of the year, we think those earnings will stabilize, and we think the market will probably catch wind of that early in 2023. So we're expecting choppiness in the near term, but we expect-- our expectation of those stable earnings should filter through into a stable market in the coming months.]

Title: Best Performing ETFs of 2022
Text: [If you guessed at the start of the year—before war, inflation and rate hikes—which funds would turn in the best annual performance, maybe you would have said broad stock indexes, real estate or bonds.You would have been wrong.The top-performing ETF of 2022, once you filter out leveraged and inverse products, was the $424.2 million iShares MSCI Turkey ETF (TUR) with a monster return of 104% through Dec. 27.Turkey’s lira plummeted during the year while inflation soared as high as 80%. However, that was what drove the stock market’s outstanding performance, as domestic investors plowed in assets to hedge against skyrocketing prices.Despite its outsized returns, U.S. investors aren’t taking the bait, and the fund has seen $82.8 million in outflows year-to-date. Indeed, a recent Bloomberg article notes that foreign ownership of Turkish stocks hit record lows.The runner up to TUR is the $375.9 million Simplify Interest Rate Hedge ETF (PFIX), which rolled out in May 2021. The fund is designed to provide a hedge against sharp increases in interest rates, which it does by holding U.S. Treasury securities and U.S. Treasury Inflation Protected Securities in conjunction with interest rate options. PFIX is up 93% this year, and unlike TUR, it has seen inflows to the tune of $123.3 million.Energy All the Way Down From PFIX on down, the top performers are energy related with one exception. The $2.6 billion VanEck Oil Services ETF (OIH) was in the No. 3 spot with a gain of 66%, followed by the $40.7 billion Energy Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLE) with a return of 65%.Ultimately the remaining energy funds in the top 20 ETFs in terms of returns were up anywhere from 49% (the Invesco DWA Energy Momentum ETF (PXI)) to 65% (the iShares U.S. Oil Equipment & Services ETF (IEZ)). Almost all of those were equity funds; however, the United States 12-Month Natural Gas Fund LP (UNL) was in the mix with a return of 57%. The fund invests in natural gas futures via a laddered strategy that maintains equal-weight exposure to the 12 nearest-month NYMEX natural gas futures.Story continuesAccording to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, energy costs for Americans saw an average increase of 13% year-over-year as of November.Nickel Another Outlier Nestled in the No. 19 spot for returns is the $43.7 million iPath Series B Bloomberg Nickel Subindex Total Return ETN (JJN) with a return of 50%. The ETN, which tracks the price of nickel futures, saw a sharp spike back in early March before falling almost as dramatically, but it climbed fairly steadily during the final quarter. Title: Best Performing ETFs of 2022
Text: [If you guessed at the start of the year—before war, inflation and rate hikes—which funds would turn in the best annual performance, maybe you would have said broad stock indexes, real estate or bonds.You would have been wrong.The top-performing ETF of 2022, once you filter out leveraged and inverse products, was the $424.2 million iShares MSCI Turkey ETF (TUR) with a monster return of 104% through Dec. 27.Turkey’s lira plummeted during the year while inflation soared as high as 80%. However, that was what drove the stock market’s outstanding performance, as domestic investors plowed in assets to hedge against skyrocketing prices.Despite its outsized returns, U.S. investors aren’t taking the bait, and the fund has seen $82.8 million in outflows year-to-date. Indeed, a recent Bloomberg article notes that foreign ownership of Turkish stocks hit record lows.The runner up to TUR is the $375.9 million Simplify Interest Rate Hedge ETF (PFIX), which rolled out in May 2021. The fund is designed to provide a hedge against sharp increases in interest rates, which it does by holding U.S. Treasury securities and U.S. Treasury Inflation Protected Securities in conjunction with interest rate options. PFIX is up 93% this year, and unlike TUR, it has seen inflows to the tune of $123.3 million.Energy All the Way Down From PFIX on down, the top performers are energy related with one exception. The $2.6 billion VanEck Oil Services ETF (OIH) was in the No. 3 spot with a gain of 66%, followed by the $40.7 billion Energy Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLE) with a return of 65%.Ultimately the remaining energy funds in the top 20 ETFs in terms of returns were up anywhere from 49% (the Invesco DWA Energy Momentum ETF (PXI)) to 65% (the iShares U.S. Oil Equipment & Services ETF (IEZ)). Almost all of those were equity funds; however, the United States 12-Month Natural Gas Fund LP (UNL) was in the mix with a return of 57%. The fund invests in natural gas futures via a laddered strategy that maintains equal-weight exposure to the 12 nearest-month NYMEX natural gas futures.Story continuesAccording to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, energy costs for Americans saw an average increase of 13% year-over-year as of November.Nickel Another Outlier Nestled in the No. 19 spot for returns is the $43.7 million iPath Series B Bloomberg Nickel Subindex Total Return ETN (JJN) with a return of 50%. The ETN, which tracks the price of nickel futures, saw a sharp spike back in early March before falling almost as dramatically, but it climbed fairly steadily during the final quarter. Demand for nickel has seen an increase largely due to its use in batteries for electric vehicles, and that demand is expected to continue to grow over the next few years. FundTickerYTD ReturniShares MSCI Turkey ETFTUR104.0%Simplify Interest Rate Hedge ETFPFIX93.0%VanEck Oil Services ETFOIH66.0%Energy Select Sector SPDR FundXLE65.2%iShares U.S. Oil Equipment & Services ETFIEZ64.9%Fidelity MSCI Energy Index ETFFENY64.4%Vanguard Energy ETFVDE64.2%Invesco Dynamic Energy Exploration & Production ETFPXE61.5%Invesco Dynamic Oil & Gas Services ETFPXJ60.9%Credit Suisse S&P MLP Index ETNMLPO60.6%SPDR S&P Oil & Gas Equipment & Services ETFXES60.6%iShares U.S. Energy ETFIYE60.2%Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight Energy ETFRYE59.7%iShares U.S. Oil & Gas Exploration & Production ETFIEO58.8%United States 12 Month Natural Gas Fund LPUNL57.1%First Trust Natural Gas ETFFCG50.3%First Trust Energy AlphaDEX FundFXN50.0%iShares Global Energy ETFIXC49.6%iPath Series B Bloomberg Nickel Subindex Total Return ETNJJN49.5%Invesco DWA Energy Momentum ETFPXI49.5%Source: FactSet, data as of Dec. 27, 2022 Contact Heather Bell at heather.bell@etf.com Recommended StoriesETF Industry’s $1T Mutual Fund Grab: Part 1 Buffered ETFs’ $10 Billion YearHot Reads: The Trouble With TechHot Reads: The Crypto Contagion ContinuesPermalink | © Copyright 2022 ETF.com. Title: Earnings: What to expect from big banks this week
Text: [Yahoo Finance Live anchors discuss the expectations for big bank earnings this week, as well as news that Goldman Sachs plans to cut 3,200 jobs.Video TranscriptBRIAN SOZZI: JPMorgan, Citigroup, Bank of America, and Wells Fargo are among the names that will be reporting their fourth-quarter earnings this Friday. Investors will be keeping an eye on how their mortgage businesses are holding up and listening for signs of optimism on the broader economy. Lots to unpack here with these bank earnings.Guys, is this the quarter where JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon again brings out the warning on the state of the economy? He certainly could. He's been, I think, very out in front warning about where this economy might go in 2023. Is it also the quarter where JPMorgan starts to pull back on some of its tech investments, given the slowing economy? So those are a couple of things I'm watching as pertains to JPM.And then, of course, on news today of Goldman cutting 3,200 jobs. We knew it was coming, but still to see it is, I would say, concerning, and how does how does that CEO, David Solomon, get on that earnings call and project his business looking forward?BRAD SMITH: Yeah, those job cuts coming after we had already seen from JP Morgan and some of the other banks as well, even prior to or during the holiday season, saying that, hey, we're going to need to roll back on some of the bonuses, and that really kind of brings into question what the total compensation package for the existing and the retained base of employees would look like going forward as the banks are really waiting for deal making to come back in full force, waiting to see where investment banking really kind of regains some type of strength given some of the equity-market declines that we had seen in last year.And so with all of that in mind, this earnings period and what they forecast, perhaps, is going to be the biggest kind of takeaway item and what they're seeing in terms of deal making and where they're going to be able to drum up some type of demand for their investment-banking products as well.Story continuesJULIE HYMAN: Yeah, when we look at the Goldman news this morning, it reminds me a little bit of what we've seen from technology because part of it is sort of a pandemic payback, if you will. That is Goldman Sachs usually does an annual culling of its underperformers. It cuts them. Didn't really do that during the pandemic. So part of this is sort of now a delayed reaction, a delayed cutting of some of those folks. That's at least some of what is going on there. But we are perhaps going to hear more about cutting from these companies, especially given that maybe they're not totally prepared for what may be coming at this point.For example, Deutsche Bank last week downgrading Bank of America, JP Morgan, and Truist saying that bank stocks have yet to fully price in a US recession. So are investors fully accounting for the effect this could have on the banks? Are the banks themselves fully accounting for the effect? I think we're going to get lots of discussion around those issues.BRIAN SOZZI: Right. It seems like there's a disconnect, Julie, because I'm looking at some Morgan Stanley price-target changes ahead of earnings. They are cutting estimates on Citigroup and Goldman Sachs pretty significantly.But if you go pull up the KBW Bank Index, as we're showing here, I mean, these stocks have gone nowhere-- really nowhere over the past year despite rising yields, and theoretically that should be good for profit margins. I would argue that chart is suggesting, you know, we're in a recession at some point this year, and that impacts a lot of the businesses beyond deal making for the banks.BRAD SMITH: It runs a little bit counter to what we typically see from some bank activity, at least, during a rising interest-rate environment. They typically would be more beneficiary where they can get more money or earn more from the difference between some of the spreads in their loans.And I think for right now, they're still trying to manage what many other businesses are in trying to understand exactly what their cost structures look like. The cut that we're seeing at Goldman is roughly double what we had seen at Morgan Stanley. That was about 1,600 employees there. And so exactly the number of people that they need in order to continue the operations or the business as usual when business right now isn't kind of that usual operating procedure, if you will, too.JULIE HYMAN: Yeah,. Just to take a step back, if you look at the big businesses of the banks, right-- net interest margin, the difference between what they put out and what they take in, basically, and what they lend, that's going to obviously be a big focus this year. Fee income related to everything from mortgage servicing to the deal making that we were talking about, all of these things are going to be in flux this year and are difficult to predict, I think.]

Title: 2023 market recalibration process will ‘take a couple quarters to play out’: Strategist
Text: [BMO Wealth Management U.S. Chief Investment Strategist Yung-Yu Ma joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss the recent relief rally in markets, potential overhangs, Fed rate hikes in 2023, and the upcoming earnings season.Video TranscriptSEANA SMITH: It's great to see you again. So today's rally I guess a bit of good news here as we round out what has certainly been a very challenging year here for the markets. What does this signal to you in terms of what investors should expect as we look ahead to 2023?YUNG-YU MA: Hi, Seana. Thanks for having me again. It is nice to have a bit of a relief rally toward the end of the year. It's been a tough year, obviously. I wouldn't read too much into today's action. There is a lot of pessimism out there. So I think that does set up the market for sort of a snap-back rally at any given time.But we are in the heart of-- or approaching the heart of the time when we're going to get earnings warnings, and so that's going to cause an overhang in the markets until we get some more clarity and until the market can see some stabilization ahead.JARED BLIKRE: Let me ask you about that because you noted something-- I'm reading your notes right here-- something that's happened in the past two quarters that centers around earnings season. I'm always interested in seasonality plays here.YUNG-YU MA: Yeah, it's been interesting. Actually the past two quarters we've seen the market carve out a short-term bottom right about two weeks after the quarter end. So really right in the heart of those earnings warnings, the market had been declining and then stabilized as the market sort of sniffed out that the actual earnings might not be that bad.So we think there's a high chance that this quarter could be a repeat of that same scenario where we struggle for a few more weeks, but as we get closer and closer to the actual earnings reporting, things actually don't seem so bad. So that's something-- a pattern to look forward to that's played out the last couple of quarters.Story continuesSEANA SMITH: So Yung-Yu, do you, I guess, look at that type of bounce-- potential bounce in the markets as a buying opportunity here for investors?YUNG-YU MA: Well, we do think selloffs here are going to be buying opportunities, and that is based on our expectation of a soft landing in 2023. We do think the labor market will remain stable. We think that inflation is going to continue to come down. Consumers will see real wage gains, and corporations are not going to cut back all that much if spending is still pretty healthy in the economy.We just think that recalibration process is going to take a couple of quarters to play out. So we do think that to the extent that we see some downturns in the equity markets over the next few months that those are probably going to be buying opportunities.JARED BLIKRE: All right, you mentioned soft landing, so we've got to talk about the Fed. Big meeting end of January, early February, I believe. What are you expecting?YUNG-YU MA: Well, the Fed has definitely signaled a difficult path ahead. We actually think the Fed is overly hawkish and overly negative in some of its projections in terms of higher inflation, slower growth, higher unemployment. We don't think that's actually going to come to pass in terms of unemployment shooting up as much as the Fed is expecting.So in the coming meeting, we think the Fed will probably soften its tone a little bit if inflation continues to come down, as it has been-- the data has actually been reasonably good for inflation-- and if we see that the labor market, at least at the edges, is softening a bit, which we are seeing, a still healthy labor market but that's softening around the edges.SEANA SMITH: So Yung-Yu, then how many more hikes do you think are likely on the table then before the Fed maybe pauses?YUNG-YU MA: Maybe another 1/2%. We think that's probably par for the course. Perhaps 1/4% the next meeting, maybe 1/2%. But overall, we think the Fed is going to pause right around 5% in terms of the fed funds rate and hold it there for quite some time.Could it be another 1/2%? Could it be another 3/4% on the upside if we get some negative inflation data? Both of those are possible, but right around 5% is where we see somewhat of a steady state for 2023.JARED BLIKRE: And when we look inside the market, what are you looking at specifically in terms of sectors, styles? Any positions that you're interested or areas of the market you're interested in the new year?YUNG-YU MA: Yeah, Jared, there definitely are. We actually think much of the plays that revolve around infrastructure have a lot of runway to them and a lot of legs. And that, of course, spans a few different sectors-- some areas of industrials, some areas of materials. But we have a lot of money that's going to flow into the economy from the Infrastructure Act, from the CHIPS Act, from the Inflation Reduction Act, and that's going to create-- you know, there are hundreds of billions of dollars of spending that are going to flow through the economy over the next few years, and we think that provides a nice runway for infrastructure.We also think biotech is probably likely to have a good year. There have been a lot of major platform developments we think are going to continue to play out in the biotech sector. So we think that's actually an area of outperformance for 2023.And I'd say a third area to pay attention to overall is just value. We think that value over growth has a long runway to it as well. So low P/E multiples, stable businesses returning cash flow or buying back shares, increasing their dividends, those areas of value that really look more stable we think have a nice trajectory to them as well.SEANA SMITH: Yung-Yu, you mentioned earnings warnings. We certainly have seen the estimates lowered for 2023. When do you expect earnings to then stabilize potentially?YUNG-YU MA: We do expect them to stabilize, and that's part of our soft-landing thesis. We think this recalibration probably has another quarter or two to go in terms of seeing pretty meaningful earnings cuts over this coming quarter and also the second quarter. But into the back half of the year, we think those earnings will stabilize, and we think the market will probably catch wind of that early in 2023. So we're expecting choppiness in the near term, but we expect-- our expectation of those stable earnings should filter through into a stable market in the coming months.]

Title: 2023 market recalibration process will ‘take a couple quarters to play out’: Strategist

What does this signal to you in terms of what investors should expect as we look ahead to 2023?YUNG-YU MA: Hi, Seana. Thanks for having me again. It is nice to have a bit of a relief rally toward the end of the year. It's been a tough year, obviously. I wouldn't read too much into today's action. There is a lot of pessimism out there. I'm always interested in seasonality plays here.YUNG-YU MA: Yeah, it's been interesting. Actually the past two quarters we've seen the market carve out a short-term bottom right about two weeks after the quarter end. So really right in the heart of those earnings warnings, the market had been declining and then stabilized as the market sort of sniffed out that the actual earnings might not be that bad.So we think there's a high chance that this quarter could be a repeat of that same scenario where we struggle for a few more weeks, but as we get closer and closer to the actual earnings reporting, things actually don't seem so bad. So that's something-- a pattern to look forward to that's played out the last couple of quarters.Story continuesSEANA SMITH: So Yung-Yu, do you, I guess, look at that type of bounce-- potential bounce in the markets as a buying opportunity here for investors?YUNG-YU MA: Well, we do think selloffs here are going to be buying opportunities, and that is based on our expectation of a soft landing in 2023. We do think the labor market will remain stable. We think that inflation is going to continue to come down. Consumers will see real wage gains, and corporations are not going to cut back all that much if spending is still pretty healthy in the economy.We just think that recalibration process is going to take a couple of quarters to play out. So we do think that to the extent that we see some downturns in the equity markets over the next few months that those are probably going to be buying opportunities.JARED BLIKRE: All right, you mentioned soft landing, so we've got to talk about the Fed. Big meeting end of January, early February, I believe. What are you expecting?YUNG-YU MA: Well, the Fed has definitely signaled a difficult path ahead. We actually think the Fed is overly hawkish and overly negative in some of its projections in terms of higher inflation, slower growth, higher unemployment. We don't think that's actually going to come to pass in terms of unemployment shooting up as much as the Fed is expecting.So in the coming meeting, we think the Fed will probably soften its tone a little bit if inflation continues to come down, as it has been-- the data has actually been reasonably good for inflation-- and if we see that the labor market, at least at the edges, is softening a bit, which we are seeing, a still healthy labor market but that's softening around the edges.SEANA SMITH: So Yung-Yu, then how many more hikes do you think are likely on the table then before the Fed maybe pauses?YUNG-YU MA: Maybe another 1/2%. We think that's probably par for the course. Perhaps 1/4% the next meeting, maybe 1/2%. But overall, we think the Fed is going to pause right around 5% in terms of the fed funds rate and hold it there for quite some time.Could it be another 1/2%? Could it be another 3/4% on the upside if we get some negative inflation data? Both of those are possible, but right around 5% is where we see somewhat of a steady state for 2023.JARED BLIKRE: And when we look inside the market, what are you looking at specifically in terms of sectors, styles? Any positions that you're interested or areas of the market you're interested in the new year?YUNG-YU MA: Yeah, Jared, there definitely are. We actually think much of the plays that revolve around infrastructure have a lot of runway to them and a lot of legs. And that, of course, spans a few different sectors-- some areas of industrials, some areas of materials. But we have a lot of money that's going to flow into the economy from the Infrastructure Act, from the CHIPS Act, from the Inflation Reduction Act, and that's going to create-- you know, there are hundreds of billions of dollars of spending that are going to flow through the economy over the next few years, and we think that provides a nice runway for infrastructure.We also think biotech is probably likely to have a good year. There have been a lot of major platform developments we think are going to continue to play out in the biotech sector. So we think that's actually an area of outperformance for 2023.And I'd say a third area to pay attention to overall is just value. We think that value over growth has a long runway to it as well. So low P/E multiples, stable businesses returning cash flow or buying back shares, increasing their dividends, those areas of value that really look more stable we think have a nice trajectory to them as well.SEANA SMITH: Yung-Yu, you mentioned earnings warnings. We certainly have seen the estimates lowered for 2023. When do you expect earnings to then stabilize potentially?YUNG-YU MA: We do expect them to stabilize, and that's part of our soft-landing thesis. We think this recalibration probably has another quarter or two to go in terms of seeing pretty meaningful earnings cuts over this coming quarter and also the second quarter. But into the back half of the year, we think those earnings will stabilize, and we think the market will probably catch wind of that early in 2023. So we're expecting choppiness in the near term, but we expect-- our expectation of those stable earnings should filter through into a stable market in the coming months.]
